Start group-kill test timeout once its child is ready (TODO 253) (#282)

TODO 253 records 1 run of tools/test-skill-release-date-client.py
that errored with FileNotFoundError for sleeper.pid in
test_a_child_that_does_not_end_is_killed_with_its_group, and 3 reruns
that passed. That is the TODO's record, not a check of this change.

The sleeper, its pid file and the probe of its pid with os.kill are
removed. The stub child now forks 1 member into its group and then
writes 1 byte to a FIFO, alive, and the client's first wait starts
only once the test reads that byte, polled for at most 60 seconds; the
poll is new to this test. The test asserts the client's reason first,
then that the byte was read when the poll ended, that the client asked
its first wait for exactly its 1 second timeout, that the real wait
lasted at least that long, and that the client's run, from its start
to its return, less the poll, ended within 15 seconds; main bounds the
whole run by 15 seconds.

End of file on alive within 10 seconds after the client returns shows
that the client killed the whole group, not only the leader: it comes
only once every process holding the write end has ended. Its time is a
clock read taken after the read that sees it, and a time past that
deadline counts as not seen. Each stub process otherwise ends by
itself 90 seconds after it enters its wait for the release, and so
more than 90 seconds after the test's start. The check takes no end of
file seen later than 85 seconds from that start, the 60 second poll,
the 15 second run and the 10 second check, plus the poll's last step,
and end of file must come before 90 seconds, or before a bound that a
caller passes in its place, so the group's own end is never taken for
the kill.

The check sends no signal. Each stub process waits for end of file on
a second FIFO, lifeline, whose only write end the test holds. The
check's finally clause closes lifeline and reaps a child the client
left unreaped if it ends within the 5 second reap grace, and the
kernel closes lifeline when the test process ends in any other way.
The stub makes 1 read of lifeline before it forks. On Linux, select
reports nothing for a FIFO reader opened with no writer, and that read
returns end of file, so a stub that starts after the release exits at
once rather than wait out its 90 seconds. A stub process past that
read ends at once on the release; one not yet there ends when it
reaches it, after the rest of its start-up, which the test does not
bound.

The stub's source ignores SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP, and Python
ignores SIGPIPE and SIGXFSZ at start-up. The stub keeps every signal
that the test thread that starts it blocks as blocked, and every
signal other than SIGCHLD, SIGPIPE and SIGXFSZ that the test process
ignores as ignored. The client changes those 3 dispositions before
exec: it resets SIGCHLD to its default in its own process, the test
process, before it starts the child, and its Popen, with its default
restore_signals, resets SIGPIPE and SIGXFSZ to their default action
in the child. SIGCHLD's default action, like ignoring it, leaves the
stub running. So, unless the test thread blocks it, SIGPIPE or SIGXFSZ
can end the stub before Python ignores it, and SIGTERM, SIGINT or
SIGHUP can end it before its source ignores it if the test process
does not ignore it.

The stub's source is a constant, GROUP_STUB. The stub first reads its
own end with float from a file, own_end, that the check writes with
str, so a plain int or float passed as own_end reaches the stub only
as a number; a text that float does not take raises before the stub
opens either FIFO, and the check fails.

The test patches client.wait_child to hold that first wait. A
client.Unavailable that the patched wait raises passes through the
client unchanged, so the check fails at its reason only when that
exception's reason is not the timeout reason; any other exception of
class Exception, or of a subclass of it, that it raises becomes an
unavailable verdict in the client that names the exception, and the
check fails at its reason; any other exception it raises, such as
KeyboardInterrupt, passes through the client and the check.

New tests run the check against a client that kills only the leader,
one that sends SIGTERM to the group, and a client whose group kill
raises KeyboardInterrupt, and assert that each fails or passes the
interrupt through and that the group then ends before the stub's own
end could come, timed from before the stub starts. Another runs it
with an own-end bound of 0.5 seconds, below the 1 second first wait
that the check asserts, and asserts that it fails at the own-end
assertion; another asserts that a stub started after the release
exits at its first read, as no ready byte shows; and another asserts,
on a stand-in clock, that an end of file seen after its deadline is
not taken. A tripwire test asserts that the only bindings of
check_group_kill, end_of_file and stub in the test file's syntax are
1 def statement
for each, counting async def, class and import statements, plain,
annotated, augmented, := and tuple or starred assignments to a name,
assignments to an attribute, a lambda so assigned, deletions, for,
with, comprehension, except and match targets, parameters and keyword
arguments, but not a name given as a string; that BoundsTest, each
class that exists when the test runs and has it among its bases,
directly or through other such classes, and each class in their method
resolution orders hold no other entry with those names, that
BoundsTest's 2 entries and the module's end_of_file are the functions
their def statements made, judged by qualified name and first line,
and that the test's instance has no such attribute of its own; that
the stub makes its pinned calls in order; and that no
name in SIGNAL_NAMES, a list of example names through which Python
code sends a signal, appears in the check, its helpers or the stub, so
a direct os.kill there fails it. The second of those assertions reads
each class and the instance through the descriptors that type and
TestCase define, not by attribute lookup, lists each namespace with
its items method, tells classes apart by identity and takes only a
plain str as 1 of those names, so these overrides, each of which
another test has a case for, hide no entry from it: a class's
__subclasses__; a metaclass's __subclasses__, __mro__, __dict__,
__eq__ or __getattribute__, the last also giving a false __qualname__;
an entry whose name is a str subclass; and an instance's __dict__
property. It does not hold against all code in the test file, which
can hide an entry by routes that the walk does not model, such as
these 2: a metaclass whose mro method puts BoundsTest in the order of
a class that does not have it among its bases, so that
type.__subclasses__ does not list that class; and a dict subclass, set
as the test's instance __dict__, whose items method leaves out an
entry.
Another test has a case for each of those forms of binding stub, for
each form of binding it by a name given as a string that the second
assertion sees on a class or an instance, for each such override, and
for 1 form that the first 2 assertions miss; its match cases run only
on Python 3.10 or later. The group-kill test asserts nothing about the
client's reap; its docstring names the 2 tests that do.

Unchanged from main: the 1 second timeout, the reason string, the
real wait, kill and reap, and a 10 second window for the group to end
after the client returns.

Reduced coverage, which landing this change accepts: the test has no
allowlist of the check's callees, no pin of the calls that start a
process with their arguments, no type test of check and own_end, no
check that they are not rebound, no check of the stub's calls for
example values of own_end, and no test that a caller's value runs no
code of its own.

Residual:

- What the tripwire's first 2 assertions miss: an edit that changes what
  self.stub finds without an entry in the classes they read or an
  attribute of the tripwire's own instance, such as a __getattribute__
  method or an assignment to self.__class__; a class derived from
  BoundsTest that does not exist when the tripwire runs, such as one in
  another module; an attribute set on an instance other than the
  tripwire's own, such as one that a subclass's setUp sets where the
  tripwire runs as BoundsTest.<test name>, not on that subclass as the
  whole file runs it; a replacement whose qualified name and first line,
  which a value gives for itself, are those of the def statement; a
  binding of check_group_kill, end_of_file or stub by a name given as a
  string anywhere other than those classes, that instance and the
  module's end_of_file; a change made after the tripwire runs or undone
  before it; an edit that rebinds a name or function the tripwire calls,
  such as class_bindings, SUBCLASSES, BoundsTest, a builtin or a
  function of ast, or that replaces the tripwire; an edit that changes
  the interpreter's own records, as through ctypes; and an entry hidden
  by a route that the walk does not model, such as a metaclass whose mro
  method puts BoundsTest in the order of a class that does not have it
  among its bases, or a dict subclass, set as the tripwire's instance
  __dict__, whose items method leaves out an entry. Code in the test
  file runs in the process that the tripwire checks, so no check there
  holds against all such code.
- What the tripwire's name scan misses: every route to a signal other
  than a name in SIGNAL_NAMES in the functions it reads. Such an edit
  passes the tripwire unless it also fails 1 of its other 3 assertions:
  it changes the stub's calls, which the STUB_CALLS pin rejects, as it
  rejects os.__dict__["kill"](os.getppid(), 0) added to the stub, or it
  binds check_group_kill, end_of_file or stub in a way the first 2
  assertions reject, as they reject a subclass of BoundsTest whose stub,
  bound by a def statement, calls getattr(os, "kill"). Passes of the
  name scan, examples, not a complete list: in check_group_kill,
  getattr(os, "kill") with a literal name, getattr with a computed name,
  such as getattr(os, "ki" + "ll"), os.__dict__["kill"],
  vars(os)["kill"] and a shell kill through os.system; a value a caller
  passes, such as the witness, which the check calls and which can run
  any code; a method of self that a subclass overrides, such as
  assertLess; a module global or builtin that a caller rebinds, such as
  GROUP_STUB, or a function of os or the client, as the tests here
  rebind os.killpg; the body of a decorator; and the code outside those
  functions, the client, whose group kill, the behaviour under test, is
  the 1 signal that a run of the group-kill test sends, and the standard
  library.
- The check takes the text of own_end with str and adds check and
  own_end, or end_bound in its place when given, to clock readings, so
  a value with methods of its own runs them in the test. str runs before
  the check reads GROUP_STUB, so a method of own_end can change the
  stub's source, for example by rebinding GROUP_STUB, and so add code to
  the stub. The callers in the test file pass numbers.
- After the release, by the finally clause or by the kernel when the
  test process ends, a stub process that has not yet reached its first
  read of lifeline ends only when it reaches that read, so it outlives
  the release, and a killed test process, by the rest of its start-up,
  which nothing in the test bounds. This is derived from the stub's
  order. The leader and the member are past that read once the ready
  byte has been read, so this arises only for a release that comes
  before the test has read that byte: during the poll, or after a poll
  that ran out without it.
- While the test process is alive but neither closes lifeline nor ends,
  as when it is stopped, each stub process lives until its own end,
  own_end seconds after it enters its wait, 90 in the group-kill test.
  It enters that wait only after start-up, its first read of lifeline
  and, for the member, the fork, so its life from its start is that
  start-up plus own_end seconds, and nothing in the test bounds the
  start-up.
- The first-wait timing passes a client whose real wait gives up early
  by less than the time the gate's 2 clock reads and the call add. The
  call's share includes the wait's overrun past its own deadline, which
  the code does not bound, so the margin is set by the host and is more
  than the 2 clock reads take.
- A process that inherits the write end of lifeline and outlives the
  test would keep the stub alive up to its own end. Only a fork without
  exec in the test process could do that: the descriptor is not
  inheritable across exec, and the test file forks only inside the
  stub's source.
- A stub process that closed its copy of alive before it ended would
  hide from the check. The stub is the test's own code, and its calls
  are pinned, so this arises only from an altered stub.
- A process that SIGKILL cannot end keeps alive open, and the check then
  fails.
- When the client gives up without reaping, the finally clause reaps the
  leader after the release if it ends within the 5 second reap grace. A
  leader that has not ended by then, or one left when the test process
  ends without unwinding, stays unreaped until Python's own collection
  of finished children or the process that adopts it reaps it. A leader
  that has ended holds no descriptor while it waits to be reaped; one
  still running, such as a stopped one, holds the descriptors it has
  open, the write end of alive among them once it has opened it.
- No signal ends the stub while it ignores or blocks that signal. Unless
  the test thread blocks it, SIGPIPE or SIGXFSZ can end the stub before
  Python ignores it, and SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGHUP can end it before its
  source ignores it if the test process does not ignore it. Examples of
  a signal that ends it early, not a complete list: SIGKILL, and SIGUSR1
  when the test neither ignores nor blocks SIGUSR1. Without such a
  signal, it ends on the release or at its own end, unless it is
  stopped, as by SIGSTOP.
- A correct client still fails the test if the child is not ready within
  60 seconds. It also fails each test that runs the check if the test
  process is delayed past 1 of the bounds the check asserts, or so long,
  after it reads the ready byte, that the stub reaches its own end
  before the client's first wait times out.
- The design needs FIFOs in the temporary folder, select on them, and
  the Linux behaviour that a FIFO reader opened while a writer exists
  sees end of file when the last writer closes. The behaviour stated
  here is that on Linux; for other platforms and for the Python 3.9
  floor it is not established.

- Add .github/squash/282.txt as the committed squash message read by
  the Pull request text gate.
